column3: A walled-in quarter of white-washed lanes in Fuzhou, once home to scholars, officials and writers, with old courtyard houses and carved doorways.
A forested mountain above Fuzhou, known for its temple, its stone inscriptions carved into the rock and its views of the city and river.
A large Buddhist temple on Drum Mountain, with halls rising up the hillside among tall trees. It has been a center of Chan Buddhism for centuries.
Fuzhou's grandest dish is a slow-cooked soup of abalone, sea cucumber, shark fin substitutes and more. Its name means Buddha Jumps Over the Wall, because even a monk could not resist the smell.
Fuzhou fish balls are springy, with a pocket of seasoned pork in the middle, and are served in a light, clear broth.
A Fuzhou delicacy, with a wrapper made by pounding lean pork into a thin, silky sheet, wrapped around a savory meat filling and served in soup.
Extremely thin, salted wheat noodles dried in long strands. They are eaten on birthdays, as a wish for a long life.
A soft, colorful stone from Shoushan that is carved into seals, animals and tiny landscapes. Fine pieces are treasured by collectors.
The local opera of Fuzhou, sung in the Fuzhou dialect, with lively tunes and a long tradition of folk tales.
A tiny car-free island off Xiamen, with winding lanes, old foreign-style villas and the sound of pianos drifting from the windows. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
A university on the seashore, with a beautiful campus of red-roofed buildings, banyan trees and a beach next to the lecture halls.
A Buddhist temple at the foot of a green hill, next to Xiamen University. Visitors come for its halls, its vegetarian restaurant and its views of the sea.
A former fishing village in Xiamen that is now a lively lane of cafés, snack stalls and small guesthouses, busy until late in the evening.
The highest point of Gulangyu, from where you can look down on red roofs, the harbor and the high-rises of Xiamen across the water.
Xiamen's signature noodles in a rich, savory broth with a peanut, shrimp and spice paste called shacha, served with seafood and pork.
A jelly made from small sea worms, boiled until they set. It is eaten cold with vinegar and garlic and is a bold local snack.
A crispy street omelet of small oysters, eggs and starch, fried in a pan and eaten with a sweet and spicy sauce.
A warm sweet soup of soft, tender peanuts, often eaten with a fried dough stick, and a typical comforting snack in Xiamen.
The Xiamen pie is a flaky, golden pastry with a sweet mung bean and sugar filling, often given as a gift.
A Fujian opera from the Quanzhou and Xiamen region, known for its funny characters, lively acting and humor.
A large temple in Quanzhou with two tall stone pagodas that stand opposite each other and have survived for about 800 years.
One of the oldest mosques in China, first built in 1009 when Quanzhou was a great port with Arab merchants. Parts of its stone gate still stand.
A long stone bridge across a tidal river, built in the 11th century. Its builders used oysters to bind the stones together.
A temple to Mazu, the goddess of the sea, who is prayed to for safe voyages. It is one of the oldest Mazu temples.
A hill north of Quanzhou with temples, rock carvings and a huge stone statue of Laozi, the founder of Daoism, said to date from the Song dynasty.
A busy old street in Quanzhou, lined with traditional shopfronts, snack stalls and the stone pagodas of Kaiyuan Temple at one end.
A thick, savory noodle soup, in which fine noodles are cooked until they melt into a gravy. It is a typical Quanzhou breakfast.
A duck slowly braised with lots of ginger and rice wine in a clay pot, warm and strong, and eaten in winter.
A thick, savory beef soup, thickened with starch and often topped with herbs and pepper.
Quanzhou's string puppets are small wooden figures moved with fine strings. They are a highly refined craft in which puppeteers perform stories in a lifelike way.
An opera of Quanzhou with a history of about 800 years, sung in the Minnan language. Its slow, graceful movements are famous.
Huge round houses of rammed earth, built by Hakka families who lived together in them. They sit among green hills and rice fields and are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
An island off the coast of Zhangzhou with white sandy beaches, rocky shores and fishing villages.
Noodles braised in a thick, savory sauce with seafood and pork, a hearty dish at weddings and festivals.
The narcissus of Zhangzhou is known across China. People grow bulbs in water and carve them, so they bloom for the New Year.
The Pinghe honey pomelo is a large, juicy and sweet pomelo, and one of the best-known fruits in Fujian.
The home island of Mazu, the sea goddess whom people across the coast and Taiwan worship. Pilgrims come to its main temple to pray for safety on the water.
Putian's version of braised noodles is cooked with clams, shrimp, pork and vegetables in a rich broth.
Lychee from Putian has been famous for a long time. Its fruit is sweet and juicy, and is harvested in early summer.
Thin rice noodles, stir-fried with seafood, mushrooms and vegetables, and a popular dish for family gatherings.
A UNESCO World Heritage Site where red cliffs rise above a winding river. It is the home of famous teas, and a favorite place to take a bamboo raft.
A tall peak in the Wuyi Mountains, reached by a steep stone staircase. The reward is a view of the winding Nine Bend Stream.
A roasted oolong tea grown among the rocky cliffs of Wuyi. Its leaves pick up the minerals of the rock, giving a deep and lasting flavor. Dahongpao is the most famous.
The first black tea in the world, born in Wuyi. Its leaves are dried over pine wood fire, which gives the tea a smoky taste.
Fresh bamboo shoots from the Wuyi hills, cut in spring and stir-fried or stewed in soup, with a crisp and sweet taste.
A flat, salted and air-dried duck from Jian'ou, which is steamed or braised. It has a rich, savory flavor and keeps for months.
The art of preparing oolong tea in Fujian. A small teapot and tiny cups are used for several quick infusions to bring out the changing flavors.
An old town in the hills with Ming-era houses, stone gates and a lake of red cliffs nearby, with few crowds.
Humble snack shops, with simple noodles, dumplings and soups, that can be found in cities all over China. They began in the small town of Shaxian.
Bamboo shoots dried in the sun of Qingliu, which are then rehydrated and stewed with meat in many dishes.
Hakka round earth houses in Yongding, among the largest in Fujian, with several floors, hundreds of rooms and a courtyard in the middle.
Known as the king of tulou, it has four concentric rings of rooms and holds hundreds of people, built over three centuries ago.
A Hakka comfort dish of tofu stuffed with seasoned minced pork, fried and gently simmered. It is often eaten at the New Year.
Vegetables dried in the sun in the Hakka region, a staple that could be kept for a long time and used all year in stews.
A mild white tea from Fuding, made from downy buds that are only withered and dried, and has a light and sweet taste.
The large yellow croaker is a prized fish in Ningde, with golden skin and tender meat. It is steamed or braised.
Pingtan is an island county whose restaurants serve just-caught crabs, shellfish and fish with simple seasonings.
The tea of the Wuyi region, known for centuries and part of its identity. It includes rock teas and black teas.
